title: Classify the Ticket
subtitle: Interpret prose into a governed category
scenario: It is 2:09 PM. You have the ticket record and the taxonomy. Now interpret: which category does TKT-4001 belong to? The customer guessed billing, but checkout being down for all users is an outage. Classify the symptom, not the guess.
input: Ticket record: TKT-4001, product Checkout, symptom "Checkout is down for all users". The customer wrote "maybe a billing problem". Taxonomy: outage (service down for many users), bug (a feature broken for some), how-to (a question), billing (invoices/payments).
instructions: Read the symptom against the taxonomy definitions.
Answer the four questions about the right category and why.

options.text: billing - the customer guessed a billing problem
outage - service is down for many users
how-to - the customer asked a question

questions.explain: Checkout down for all users matches the outage definition (service down for many). The customer's billing guess is a distractor; classify the symptom.

questions.prompt: Why not classify it as the customer's guess (billing)?

options.text: Because you classify the observed symptom, not the guessed cause
Because billing tickets are never urgent

questions.explain: Classification maps the symptom (what is happening) to the taxonomy. The customer's cause is a hypothesis, not the category.

questions.prompt: What makes 'outage' the right call over 'bug'?

options.text: 'All users' means many are affected - the outage definition, not a bug for some
There is no difference between them

questions.explain: The definitions decide: outage is 'down for many users'; a bug is 'broken for some'. 'All users' puts this squarely in outage.

questions.prompt: Which steps consume this category next?

options.text: Priority assignment and route decision both read the category
None - classification is the last step

questions.explain: The category feeds priority (impact) and routing (queue). A wrong category here misroutes everything downstream.

copilotPrompt: Classify a support ticket against a governed taxonomy: map the reported symptom (checkout down for all users) to the right category (outage), not the customer's guessed cause (billing).
successMessage: Ticket classified as outage. You mapped the symptom to the taxonomy, not the customer's guess.

sections.title: The human-text-to-signal step
sections.body: Classification is where messy customer prose becomes a structured signal. It is judgement, but disciplined judgement: you map to defined categories, not to gut feel.

sections.title: Symptom over cause
sections.body: Customers narrate causes ('maybe billing'). Your job is the symptom ('checkout down'). Reading the symptom against the definitions is what keeps classification consistent across agents.

sections.title: Definitions settle it
sections.body: When two categories seem to fit, the definitions break the tie. 'Many users' vs 'some users' is exactly why this is an outage, not a bug.

sections.title: What you produce here
sections.body: A classification the priority and routing steps read. It is the highest-leverage - and highest-risk - interpretation in the pipeline.

realWorld.soloRebuildPath: You'd read the ticket, match the symptom to your category definitions, and tag it - not just echo the customer's words.

takeaway.heading: Ticket classified
points: You mapped the symptom to the outage category against the definitions.
You classified what is happening, not the customer's guessed cause.
'All users' vs 'some users' made outage the right call over bug.
Priority and routing both read this category next.
The workflow can now turn ticket prose into a governed category.
